passage: The stream-selection form was due on Monday, and Ojas, sixteen, still hadn't filled it in. Money was tight since his father's shop had closed, and entrance coaching cost more than they had. On Saturday he sat in his uncle Uday's two-wheeler repair shop, handing him spanners. Uday Mama noticed that Ojas could hear a bad spark plug before he saw it. "You've always had the ear for engines," he said. Ojas turned a spanner over in his hands. On the back of the form he listed: good at fixing, bad at sitting still, likes explaining to customers, hates cramming. Then two columns: diploma in automobile engineering, or science stream. "The diploma fits more of me," he said slowly. "But I want to check with the school counsellor first."

qa.q: When was the stream-selection form due?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: What was Ojas thinking as he turned the spanner over?
qa.a: He was weighing Uday Mama's comment against his own strengths and doubts, trying to see which path fits who he is.

qa.q: Why is checking with the school counsellor a sensible next step?
qa.a: A counsellor can give accurate information about the diploma and other options, so his choice rests on facts, not only feelings.

qa.q: How might Uday Mama feel seeing Ojas consider an engine-related path?
qa.a: Proud that his nephew's skill was noticed, though he may also want Ojas to choose freely rather than copy him.

grounding: It shows a teenager weighing his strengths against possible careers under a deadline and money pressure.

passage: In a busy physiotherapy clinic on the second floor of a Pune building, Sudha, fifteen, spent a summer Saturday shadowing her neighbour, Dilnaz Aunty. She watched Dilnaz coax an old man to lift his arm an inch higher, laughing with him, patient as water. Sudha had always said she'd be a doctor, because everyone in her family said it. But she hated the sight of blood, and she loved talking to people. By lunch she had helped three patients fill in their forms and made an elderly lady laugh. On the bus home she opened her notes and wrote: "Like: people, movement, slow progress. Don't like: blood, emergencies." Then, underneath: "Physio? Occupational therapy? Ask Dilnaz Aunty what she studied."

qa.q: How many patients did Sudha help with forms?
qa.a: Three patients.

qa.q: Why did Sudha start doubting her plan to be a doctor?
qa.a: She realised it came from her family's expectations, while her own likes and dislikes, like hating blood, pointed elsewhere.

qa.q: What makes Sudha's likes-and-dislikes list a useful tool?
qa.a: It turns a vague feeling into clear points she can match against real jobs.

qa.q: How might Sudha's family react to her new ideas?
qa.a: They may be surprised or even disappointed at first, since they expected her to become a doctor.

grounding: It shows a teenager imagining career paths and testing them against her own strengths after shadowing someone at work.

"Papa, I don't want to leave the farm. I just don't want to farm the way we do now."
Jagdish put down his cup. "What does that mean, Mohit?"
"I want to study agricultural science. Soil testing, water, all of it."
"You're good at maths. Your teacher said engineering."
"I'm good at maths, but I'm happiest out here. Remember when I fixed the drip line last year? I stayed up reading about it for a week."
"Engineering pays more."
"Maybe. But I'd hate it, and I'd be bad at what I hate."
Jagdish was quiet. "And if the college is far?"
"Then I come back every harvest. And afterwards I come back with what I learned."
"Write down the colleges. We'll look together."

qa.q: What did Mohit fix last year?
qa.a: The drip line.

qa.q: What was Jagdish probably feeling when he went quiet?
qa.a: Torn between hoping for a better-paying job for Mohit and seeing how much Mohit loves the farm.

qa.q: Which part of Mohit's argument was most convincing, and why?
qa.a: Linking his maths strength with where he is happiest, using the drip line as proof, showed the choice was thought through.

qa.q: How might Mohit's teacher see this choice?
qa.a: The teacher may have pictured engineering as the best use of Mohit's maths, without knowing how much the farm matters to Mohit.

grounding: It shows a teenager matching strengths and interests to a possible career and discussing it with a parent.

passage: A year ago I was sure I'd be an architect, because everyone said I draw well. Then my aunt Jaya, who runs a small bakery in Kochi, let me help during the Christmas rush. "Elizabeth, you're on orders," she said. I didn't draw anything for two weeks. I counted orders, calmed an angry customer, and fixed the delivery list when two boys didn't turn up. By the end I noticed I was happiest not with the icing but when the chaos ran smoothly. So I made a list in two columns: what I'm good at, and what different jobs actually need. Drawing was there, but so were planning and talking to strangers. Now I'm looking at hotel management and event planning too. I haven't decided. But I've stopped picking a future just because it matched one compliment.

qa.q: Where is Aunt Jaya's bakery?
qa.a: It is in Kochi.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth notice about when she felt happiest?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt happiest when the busy rush ran smoothly, which was a surprise, since drawing had seemed to be the thing.

qa.q: How could a school counsellor support Elizabeth now?
qa.a: A counsellor could help Elizabeth explore a few fields that match the list and set up talks or short visits with people in those jobs.

qa.q: How might Aunt Jaya have seen Elizabeth during the rush?
qa.a: Aunt Jaya probably saw a dependable helper who handled problems calmly, and may have been glad to give her that experience.

grounding: Shows a teenager testing an assumed career against real experience and a list of her strengths.

passage: Counsellor's note, Class 10 career week. Devika came to my table twice. The first time she said, 'My parents want engineering, and I'm fine at maths, so.' She didn't look at me. The second time, after the session with the wildlife researcher, she came back with her friend Dilnaz and a page of questions: which subjects, how much fieldwork, whether the pay is steady. She rated herself honestly: strong in biology, patient, 'bad with heat, but I could get used to it.' Dilnaz pointed out that Devika spends every Sunday at the bird sanctuary with her grandfather. Devika laughed but didn't deny it. Next step: I have given her two books on careers in ecology and suggested she discuss both paths at home with her question sheet in hand.

qa.q: What did Devika say the first time she came to the table?
qa.a: That her parents want engineering and she is fine at maths.

qa.q: What does Devika not looking at the counsellor the first time suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was unsure or unexcited about the choice she was repeating.

qa.q: Why is suggesting she take the question sheet home a helpful step?
qa.a: It lets her talk with her parents using concrete facts about both paths, instead of arguing from feelings alone.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz seem to see Devika's interests?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees her friend's love of birds clearly and nudges her to take it seriously as a possible career.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager weighing her own strengths and interests against possible careers during career week.

passage:
Uma's diary, Friday
Career day at school. My brother Darshan says I should do engineering "because you're good at maths". I'm okay at maths. But today, at the architecture stall, I couldn't stop looking at the model of a school with a courtyard. I made a list tonight. Strengths: drawing, patience, noticing small things, okay maths. Things I love: buildings, little kids. Things I hate: sitting still for hours. So maybe architecture. Or maybe teaching. Maybe something that mixes both, like designing schools? I'm fifteen, so I don't have to decide yet, but it felt good to think about it properly.

qa.q: What model did Uma keep looking at?
qa.a: A model of a school with a courtyard.

qa.q: How did Uma feel after making the list?
qa.a: Uma felt hopeful and clearer, glad to think about the future on Uma's own terms.

qa.q: What could Uma try next to test these ideas?
qa.a: Talk to an architect or a teacher, or try a short course, to see what the work is really like.

qa.q: How might Darshan react to Uma's list?
qa.a: Darshan might be surprised, but could respect that Uma is choosing based on real strengths.

grounding: Shows a teenager imagining career paths and weighing personal strengths against them.

passage: In the small town, Mridul, sixteen, spent his holidays at his aunt Yamini's electronics repair shop. He could fix a radio faster than her other helper, and customers started asking for him. "You have good hands and a patient head," Yamini said. At home, everyone expected him to go to engineering college. One evening, soldering a loose wire, he wondered: did he want to design circuits, or fix things people needed tomorrow? He liked the people who came in, grateful. He liked seeing the problem in his hands. He started asking Yamini about the diploma course she'd done, and what she'd do differently.

qa.q: Whose shop did Mridul spend his holidays at?
qa.a: His aunt Yamini's electronics repair shop.

qa.q: What was Mridul thinking about while soldering the wire?
qa.a: He felt curious and a little torn, wondering whether he wanted to design circuits or fix things for people.

qa.q: What would you advise Mridul as he weighs his options?

passage: On careers day at the Manchester sixth-form college, Bilal walked past the stalls with his friend Soo-ah. Law, medicine, finance. Nothing clicked. Then he stopped at the engineering apprenticeship table, where a woman was showing a small engine taken apart. "I fix my cousin's bikes," Bilal said. "Every weekend." "Do you enjoy it?" "I forget to eat when I'm doing it." Soo-ah laughed. "True." Bilal picked up a gear, turning it. "But my maths isn't great." "Some of the course is maths," the woman said, "and a lot is hands-on." That evening Bilal wrote two lists: things he's good at, things he's bad at. Fixing things sat at the top.

qa.q: What was the woman at the table showing?
qa.a: A small engine taken apart.

qa.q: How did Bilal feel when he picked up the gear?
qa.a: He felt interested and hopeful, but still worried about his maths.

qa.q: What could Bilal do next to test this career idea?
qa.a: He could ask to shadow a mechanic or engineer, and talk to a teacher about support for the maths part.

qa.q: How does Soo-ah see Bilal's interest in fixing things?
qa.a: Soo-ah seems to know it well and agrees he truly loves it.

grounding: At a careers day, a teenager matches his love of fixing bikes to a possible engineering path.

passage: In the counsellor's room at the Nashik school, Jaya, fifteen, stared at the results of her aptitude test. "Social work? I wanted to be a doctor." Tanuja Ma'am, the counsellor, smiled. "The test isn't a verdict. What do you like about medicine?" "Helping people. And my parents want it." "What do you like doing now?" Jaya thought. "I help my neighbour's kids with homework. I organised the flood collection drive." "And biology?" Jaya made a face. "I get through it." Tanuja Ma'am nodded. "Then maybe look at both. Talk to a social worker and a doctor this month." Jaya folded the report into her bag, still frowning, but thinking.

qa.q: What career did the aptitude test suggest?
qa.a: Social work.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she stared at the results?
qa.a: She felt surprised and confused, because it didn't match the plan of becoming a doctor.

qa.q: What did Tanuja Ma'am suggest Jaya do next?
qa.a: Talk to a social worker and a doctor this month, to compare what each job is really like.

qa.q: How might Jaya's parents react if she brings up social work?
qa.a: They might be surprised or worried, since they want her to study medicine.

Dear Hafsa Didi,
Ammi says you're working double shifts at the hospital, so reply whenever. I've been thinking about what I want to do after Class 12. Everyone says engineering, because I'm okay at maths. But when Dadi was in hospital last year, I watched you, how calm you were, how you knew what to do. I kept thinking, I want to be that useful. But I faint at blood. Is that a problem for nursing? I'm good at staying calm and explaining things, but not at long hours. What do you actually do all day? What's the hardest part? I don't want to pick a job just because it's safe or because it's what everyone says.
Your cousin brother,
Yash

qa.a: Because Hafsa is working double shifts at the hospital.

qa.q: How does Yash feel about choosing a career after Class 12?
qa.a: He feels uncertain and torn between the safe choice of engineering and wanting to be useful like Hafsa.

qa.q: What might help Yash decide whether nursing suits him?

You want to know how I picked electrical work? Honestly, Gopika, it picked me a bit. In Class 9 I told everyone I'd be a doctor, because that's what toppers say. Then biology practicals started and I felt nothing. Zero.
Meanwhile our building's inverter kept dying, and I was the one opening it up with the watchman, reading the manual, asking the repair uncle a hundred questions. I'd lose three hours and not notice.
So I made a list. What am I good at? Patient with wires, good with my hands, bad with blood. What jobs use that? Electrician, electrical engineer, solar installer.
My parents were worried at first. I'm still Charu, still stubborn. But now when I talk about my future, I sound like myself.

qa.a: That Charu would be a doctor, because that's what toppers say.

qa.q: What does Charu losing three hours over the inverter suggest about Charu's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Charu felt absorbed and genuinely interested in a way biology never did.

qa.q: What could Charu do next to test the list of possible jobs?
qa.a: Charu could spend a day with a solar installer or electrician, or try a short course, to see how the real work feels.

qa.q: How might Charu's parents have seen Charu's change of plan?
qa.a: They were worried at first, perhaps because doctor sounded safer, but they may come round as they see how excited Charu is.

passage:
Farida here, from the flat opposite. I've watched Pankaj on his balcony all summer.
In May he was always on a laptop with a sketchbook beside it. His mother told mine he wanted to design games. Then in June he started sitting with his grandfather's old radio, taking it apart. He'd hold up tiny pieces and squint.
One evening I heard him on the phone: "Maybe I don't want to make games. Maybe I want to make the things games run on."
By July he had two columns taped to the window: GOOD AT and JOBS. I couldn't read it all, but I saw "soldering" and "patience" crossed out and rewritten.
I don't know what he's decided. He looks less stressed than in May, though, and he hums while he works.

qa.q: What did Pankaj tape to the window by July?
qa.a: Two columns: GOOD AT and JOBS.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have been feeling when he said he wanted to make the things games run on?
qa.a: He probably felt a mix of doubt and excitement, unsure of his first plan and curious about building hardware instead.

qa.q: How could a parent support Pankaj's search?
qa.a: A parent could ask about his two columns and help him meet someone who builds electronics, without pushing either plan.

qa.q: How does Farida see Pankaj's summer?
qa.a: Farida sees his work change and notices he looks less stressed and hums, though she admits she doesn't know what he has decided.

passage: Mridul, you keep asking your Deepika Bua how she ended up designing bridges. At sixteen I was sure I'd be a doctor, because my father and everyone at the dinner table said so. That summer I volunteered at the clinic in our town and fainted at the first blood test I watched. I cried the whole way home. My friend Salma dragged me to the river instead, and I spent the afternoon asking why the old railway bridge hadn't fallen in the floods. That night I made two columns: things I'm good at, and things I love. Maths and drawing were in both. Blood was in neither. I told my father the next week. He was quiet for a long time, then asked to see my drawings.
